prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength reveal and control quantum systems at fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep B030 as a single-part prize and my view is firmer after round 1, for scientific reasons. The core is a clean physical idea: at the magic wavelength the trapping light shifts the ground and excited clock states equally, so the lattice stops perturbing the transition. What followed was the careful, detail-by-detail control of blackbody, collisional and lattice shifts that I value in experiments. The result has been reproduced and surpassed independently in Tokyo, Boulder, Paris, Braunschweig and elsewhere, with clock-to-clock comparisons agreeing near 10^-18, so the accuracy claim is robust rather than one group's. It has opened a regime that was not accessible before: relativistic redshift resolved over millimetres, bounds on drifts of constants and ultralight dark matter, and many-body spin physics in a clock. This directly answers the chair's question on 'discovery or invention': the statute names both, and I read this as an invention that has also been a discovery engine, whose physics rests on a concrete mechanism and not on a technology payoff. The citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice clock and its realization and say nothing about the redefinition of the second, so that it is clearly separate from the 2005 frequency-comb prize (a ruler for optical frequencies) and the 2012 prize (control and measurement of single quantum systems, including the Al+ ion clock). The lattice clock interrogates thousands of neutral atoms at once with the motion frozen by the lattice, which is a different regime of statistical power and many-body control. The attribution is the least contested on the shortlist: Katori proposed the scheme and first demonstrated it, and Ye took it to the accuracy and many-body regime. On the share question, I would describe it in the citation as joint credit for invention and realization and not try to weight the two. I do not accept that the SI redefinition should carry weight in the decision; it is context and not the basis.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is a real objection, and a strict reader could call the lattice clock a very successful refinement of precision spectroscopy and not a new phenomenon. Its payoff for fundamental physics so far consists of bounds, not detections: no variation of constants and no dark-matter signal has been seen, and the redshift measurements confirm general relativity. Credit outside the pair is also real: Lemonde's group, Hollberg, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and others made important early contributions, and a two-name prize leaves them out. Finally, I am an interested party in the quantum-technology community, and I should be careful not to overvalue a platform because I admire the discipline of its experimentalists. I weigh these as real but not decisive.

responses.point: Olsson asks that applications be kept out of the citation, questions whether a metrology record is a discovery in the statutory sense, and discloses her Tokyo fellowship and exchanges with the university where Katori is based, flagging possible recusal on B030.
responses.response: I agree with keeping applications out of the citation; it is also the best way to protect the prize from the 'technology' reading and from the unfinished SI redefinition. On discovery versus invention, I think her own test, whether the credited people did the original work, is met here. On her disclosure, I do not think an institutional fellowship without collaboration or personal tie requires recusal, and I would be content to treat it as noted and not as a bar. If other members feel differently I would defer to the chair, but I would not want her scientific judgment on atomic metrology removed from the vote for this reason alone.

responses.point: Kroll argues the SI redefinition discussion makes recognition current, and asks how to divide credit between Katori's concept and first demonstration and Ye's accuracy and many-body work, noting that Lemonde's group and others are outside the credited names.
responses.response: I said earlier that the redefinition strengthens the case, and after reading Olsson and Pearce I now think that overstated it: the scientific case stands without it, and I would not argue about timing at all. On credit, I would resist ranking the two contributions. The concept without the 10^-18 realization, or the realization without the magic-wavelength idea, would not have produced this clock. Where I think we should be candid is in the committee record: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and others have genuine early claims. The three-name limit is not the problem here, since the pair is accepted by all proposers, but I support asking expert reviewers to confirm that no priority claim for the first lattice-clock demonstration is strong enough to change the credited names.

responses.point: Pearce moved from IceCube (B020) to B030 and has not found a second, distinct part that fits within the three-person limit. He also notes Kroll's and Johansson's view that IceCube source identification is still thin.
responses.response: I appreciate that the chair moved on scientific grounds, and I agree that I have not found a workable second part either. B020 is the strongest alternative but a pairing with B030 would need Halzen, Karle and Spiering, which is three names on its own and breaks the limit for the whole configuration. A second part also needs to be both distinct and fairly attributed, and I see no candidate meeting both. On IceCube, I accept his correction: the diffuse flux is secure in several channels, and my earlier concern was about source identification, which concerns a later chapter and not the discovery. That moves B020 up in my alternatives, but I still find no honest way to credit hundreds of contributors with three names.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers precision CMB mapping (B055), argues the measurement side was deliberately left open after COBE and the 2019 prize, and says he would not be unhappy to see B030 win.
responses.response: His candour about the thin support and the Page versus Puget and WMAP versus Planck problem is what a committee needs. The CMB parameters are secure, and I am happy to defer to him on cosmology. Where I differ is on whether a precision refinement of a quantity the committee has already honoured twice, through COBE and the 2019 prize, is a stronger discovery than the lattice clock; I think it is not, and the unresolved name set matters here. He is also right that I cannot judge the WMAP and Planck priority question. I would not want to see B055 awarded with an arbitrary third name, and I take his stated willingness to accept B030 as confirmation that it is the position with the broadest scientific support.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers the KPZ universality class (B049) for Kardar and Zhang, values its simple mechanism and exact results, and acknowledges that Parisi, a co-author and laureate, is not among the credited names and that nobody else ranked it.
responses.response: I find the physical case attractive, and the exact one-dimensional results and Tracy-Widom statistics are exactly the kind of unexpected generality I like in a theory. My difficulty is the one he names himself: a prize to two of the three 1986 authors, with the third already a laureate, would need a citation that explains the omission, and Zhang has died, which complicates the name set further. The experimental confirmation is also narrower than the reach of the theory. I do not think that sinks the candidate, but it keeps B049 from being the configuration I could defend publicly, and I note that he lists B030 as his own alternative. I would like to hear whether the attribution problem changes his rank.

responses.point: Eriksson moved to B030 from topological insulators (B058), but says a new state of matter is arguably deeper than an instrument and would not object if the committee valued that more. Several members raise the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang omission from the Kane, Mele and Molenkamp trio.
responses.response: I agree that topological insulators are the deepest physics among the competing candidates, and my own reservation on B058 is not the science. It is the combination of the 2016 topology prize and the three-name limit, which forces us to leave out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang's HgTe prediction, the very work that guided Molenkamp's experiment. That omission is hard to defend. If an expert report showed a defensible trio, I would reconsider and might place B058 above B020 in my alternatives. As things stand, the clock configuration has a cleaner credit story, which is the deciding factor and not a judgment that an instrument is deeper than a new class of matter.

uncertainties: Whether expert reviewers find a priority claim (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and others) strong enough to change or qualify the two-name credit.

Whether the committee accepts a precision-measurement invention as a discovery or invention in the statutory sense, given the 2005 and 2012 prizes, even with a citation worded narrowly around the magic-wavelength lattice clock.
Whether a distinct and fairly attributed second part exists within the three-person limit; I have not found one, and B020 and B058 are both blocked by attribution.
How much of the clock's reach into fundamental physics is demonstrated versus prospective; today it consists of bounds and redshift confirmations, not new-physics detections.
statement.conflict_note: I am Director of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and a theorist in superconducting circuits. That gives me a clear connection to B029 (circuit QED) and a lesser one to B044 (quantum computing theory). In answer to the chair's question, I confirm that I would recuse myself from any vote that involves B029 and would ask the committee to discount my earlier ranking of it; my preferred configuration and alternatives no longer involve B029. I have no personal, collaborative or institutional connection to Katori or Ye apparent from my profile, so I see no conflict on B030. I note Kroll's WACQT role and Olsson's and Mehlig's Chalmers/Gothenburg environment as institutional proximity only; none of us has any tie to the credited names in B030.
